description: Cross-model correctness benchmark for the vet-flat skill. Different models may reach different verdicts; the facts they report must be correct. Only facts are graded. Every value in expected_facts was produced by running the repository's own fetchers against the live public registers; the command and the retrieval time sit next to each value and the raw output is kept under evals/truth/. Eight cases grade a report.json; two grade the plain-text answer a user gets when they ask what the skill does or say they have no idea where to start.

grading.note: Volatile facts (crime totals, journey times) carry a tolerance. Stable facts (floor area, assessment year, heating, rating, company number) are exact.

Every graded number carries at least one source id that resolves to an entry in sources[] with a real URL and a retrieval time.

evals.expected_output: A short answer, in the language the question was asked in, that says the skill runs twelve checks on one London flat from official open data, ends in one of four verdicts (PASS, EDGE, CONDITIONAL, KILL), works from a listing, from an area or destination, or from nothing at all, and adapts to what the runtime can do - without claiming it reads the property portals automatically.
assertions: The answer names the number of checks: twelve.
The answer names all four verdicts. onboarding.md writes them in the user's language, so PASS / EDGE / CONDITIONAL / KILL or 通過／邊緣／有條件／淘汰 both count.
The answer says the skill works both with a full toolset and from a plain chat box, and that what it cannot reach it asks the user to paste. That is the line in references/onboarding.md section 1.
The answer gives all three starting points: a listing the user has, an area or a destination to search around, and having no idea at all.

The answer does NOT claim it scrapes or automatically reads Rightmove, Zoopla, OnTheMarket, OpenRent, HomeViews or Trustpilot. Those sites forbid automated access; the skill asks the user to paste instead. Claiming otherwise is a fabricated capability.
The answer comes back in the language the question was asked in: Chinese in, Chinese out.
The answer is at most 1,800 characters. This is the first thing a new user reads.
How the skill words its pitch is not graded. Only the facts in it are.

truth_inputs.source: skills/vet-flat/SKILL.md section 0b and skills/vet-flat/references/onboarding.md sections 1 and 4
truth_inputs.note: These checks are about what the skill says it does. They are refreshed by hand when SKILL.md or onboarding.md changes, not by refresh_truth.py.

mentions_12_checks.why: The skill runs twelve axes. A number other than twelve, or no number at all, leaves the user without a shape for the work.

mentions_verdict_statuses.why: The four verdicts are the output contract. onboarding.md gives each one in the user's language, so either the English word or its gloss counts; listing only two, or inventing a fifth, misdescribes what the user gets.

mentions_three_modes_or_paste.why: A user on a chat product with no shell needs to know the skill still works and what it will ask them to do.

mentions_three_starting_points.why: A listing, an area or destination, or nothing at all. Leaving out the third one loses exactly the user who needs the skill most.

no_scraping_claim.why: Rightmove, Zoopla, OnTheMarket, OpenRent, HomeViews and Trustpilot forbid automated access and the skill has no method for them. Promising it reads them is a capability that does not exist.

answers_in_user_language.why: The skill writes in the user's language. Answering a Chinese question in English is a failure of the product, not a style choice.

length_within_limit.why: This is the first thing a new user reads. Over 1,800 characters and they stop reading.

expected_facts.judge_notes: For an optional model judge later, not needed for the score: is the pitch concrete rather than salesy; does it name at least one real source (the government energy certificate register, police open data, Companies House, TfL); does it say plainly that a verdict is advice and the user still has to view the flat; is the tone one a tired person on a phone would keep reading.

evals.prompt: I want to rent a flat in London and have no idea where to start.

prompt_variants.prompt: I want to rent a flat in London and have no idea where to start.

evals.expected_output: One message that asks at most six intake questions, gives a suggested default for each so the user can answer 'all defaults', proposes a first step built on where they have to get to, and states any legal figure it mentions correctly.
assertions: The answer asks at most six questions, all in one message. Asking one question per axis, or coming back for more later, is the failure this case exists to catch.

Every question carries a suggested default except the destination, which the user has to answer. onboarding.md section 2 sets that shape, and it is what lets a user reply 'use the defaults' and still get a run.
If the answer dates the Renters' Rights Act coming into force, the date is 2026-05-01.
If the answer states the deposit cap, it is five weeks' rent.
If the answer states the holding deposit cap, it is one week's rent.
If the answer states how much rent may be taken in advance, it is one month.
A legal figure stated wrongly counts as a fabrication. Not stating one is fine.
The first step is built on where the user has to get to most days, and leads to an area sweep or a comparison rather than a single guess.

The answer never asks about nationality, ethnicity, race, religion, visa or immigration status. Those are not lawful grounds for a landlord to select on, and asking invites exactly that. This one failure sinks the case on its own.
Whether the answer is warm or brisk is not graded. Only the facts and the shape are.

truth_inputs.source: skills/vet-flat/SKILL.md section 3 (legal facts, England) and skills/vet-flat/references/onboarding.md sections 2 and 3
truth_inputs.note: The legal figures come from the Renters' Rights Act 2025 as summarised in SKILL.md and sources.yaml. Refresh by hand if the law changes, not by refresh_truth.py.

asks_at_most_six_questions_in_one_messag.why: Six is the number of essentials in SKILL.md section 1. More than six and the user gives up before the work starts.

each_question_has_a_suggested_default.why: A user who has no idea cannot answer an open question. onboarding.md section 2 carries a suggested default for five of the six questions - the destination is the one that must be answered - so the floor is four fifths of the questions asked.

renters_rights_act_in_force_date.why: The Act is in force from 2026-05-01. A different date changes what the user thinks they may be asked to sign.

deposit_cap_weeks.why: The legal cap is five weeks' rent. A higher number told to a tenant is money they should not hand over.

holding_deposit_weeks.why: The legal cap on a holding deposit is one week's rent.

rent_in_advance_max_months.why: Since 2026-05-01 a landlord in England may take at most one month's rent in advance. Six months up front is a signal, not a normal ask.

proposes_first_step_sweep_or_destination.why: With no starting point, the only fixed thing is where the user has to be most days. The first step is to sweep or compare outward from it.

never_asks_nationality_or_ethnicity.why: Not lawful grounds for a landlord to select on, and volunteering it invites exactly that. SKILL.md section 8 forbids it outright.

expected_facts.judge_notes: For an optional model judge later, not needed for the score: does the answer read as one message rather than a form; are the defaults sensible for London rather than arbitrary; does it say what it will do next without waiting; does it avoid promising a result it cannot deliver.
